claim: Cytoplasmic extracts predominantly from Xenopus eggs have made major contributions to the initial discovery and characterization of the central cell-cycle regulators including the protein complex cyclin B1-Cdk1.
source: Cytoplasmic extracts predominantly from Xenopus eggs (Murray, 1991) have made major contributions to the initial discovery and characterization of the central cell-cycle regulators including the protein complex cyclin B1-Cdk1 (Masui and Markert, 1971; Murray et al., 1989; Lohka and Maller, 1985; Lohka et al., 1988)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work that discovered and characterized cyclin B1-Cdk1 using Xenopus egg extracts.

claim: Cytoplasmic extracts predominantly from Xenopus eggs have made major contributions to the initial discovery and characterization of the anaphase-promoting complex or cyclosome (APC/C).
source: Cytoplasmic extracts predominantly from Xenopus eggs (Murray, 1991) have made major contributions to the initial discovery and characterization of the central cell-cycle regulators including the protein complex cyclin B1-Cdk1 (Masui and Markert, 1971; Murray et al., 1989; Lohka and Maller, 1985; Lohka et al., 1988) and the anaphase-promoting complex or cyclosome (APC/C) (Sudakin et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sudakin et al., 1995, which discovered/characterized APC/C using Xenopus extracts.

claim: Cell-free extracts have been used to investigate downstream mitotic events such as spindle assembly and chromosome segregation.
source: Cell-free extracts have also been used to investigate downstream mitotic events such as spindle assembly and chromosome segregation (Hannak and Heald, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hannak and Heald, 2006.

claim: Detailed dissections of the regulatory circuits in Xenopus extracts have revealed architecture of interlinked positive and negative feedbacks.
source: Moreover, detailed dissections of the regulatory circuits in these extracts have revealed architecture of interlinked positive and negative feedbacks (Kumagai and Dunphy, 1992; Mueller et al., 1995; Yang and Ferrell, 2013; Chang and Ferrell, 2013; Trunnell et al., 2011; Kim and Ferrell, 2007; Pomerening et al., 2005; Pomerening et al., 2003; Novak and Tyson, 1993; Thron, 1996)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies that dissected regulatory circuits in Xenopus extracts.

claim: Interlinked feedback loops are found in many other biological oscillators.
source: Such interlinked feedback loops are also found in many other biological oscillators (Rust et al., 2007; Hoffmann et al., 2002; Cross, 2003; Lee et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies of other biological oscillators.

claim: Interlinked feedback loops have been shown computationally to play an important role in achieving the essential clock functions such as robustness and tunability.
source: Such interlinked feedback loops are also found in many other biological oscillators (Rust et al., 2007; Hoffmann et al., 2002; Cross, 2003; Lee et al., 2000) and have been shown computationally to play an important role in achieving the essential clock functions such as robustness and tunability (Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2008, which performed computational studies.

claim: Bulk cell-free systems lack the essential single-cell information to understand a class of out-of-steady-state dynamics including cell cycles.
source: Bulk cell-free systems, despite having unique advantages of manipulation and characterization of biochemical networks, lack the essential single-cell information to understand a class of out-of-steady-state dynamics including cell cycles.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reasoning about the limitations of bulk systems for studying out-of-steady-state dynamics.

claim: Oscillations generated in well-mixed bulk solutions tend to produce quickly damped oscillations.
source: However, one major limitation for most in vitro reconstitutions up to date is that oscillations are generated in well-mixed bulk solutions, which tend to produce quickly damped oscillations (Pomerening et al., 2005; Nakajima et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pomerening et al., 2005 and Nakajima et al., 2005.

claim: Bulk reactions lack the similarity to the actual cell dimensions and the ability of mimicking spatial organization achieved by functional compartmentalization in real cells.
source: Additionally, these bulk reactions lack the similarity to the actual cell dimensions and the ability of mimicking spatial organization achieved by functional compartmentalization in real cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reasoning about the limitations of bulk reactions compared to cellular systems.

claim: The authors developed an artificial cell cycle system by encapsulating reaction mixtures containing cycling Xenopus egg cytoplasm in cell-scale micro-emulsions.
source: To overcome these challenges, we developed an artificial cell cycle system by encapsulating reaction mixtures containing cycling Xenopus egg cytoplasm (Murray, 1991) in cell-scale micro-emulsions.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental approach developed by the authors.

claim: The droplet-based artificial cells are stable for days.
source: These droplet-based cells are stable for days and keep oscillating for dozens of cycles, offering large gains in high-throughput and long-term tracking of dynamical activities in individual droplets.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations of droplet stability.

claim: The droplet-based artificial cells keep oscillating for dozens of cycles.
source: These droplet-based cells are stable for days and keep oscillating for dozens of cycles, offering large gains in high-throughput and long-term tracking of dynamical activities in individual droplets.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations of oscillations in droplets.

claim: The authors successfully reconstituted a series of mitotic events including chromosome condensation, nuclear envelope breakdown and destruction of anaphase substrates such as the proteins securin and cyclin B1.
source: In this system, we successfully reconstituted a series of mitotic events including chromosome condensation, nuclear envelope breakdown and destruction of anaphase substrates such as the proteins securin and cyclin B1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations of mitotic events in their system.

claim: The oscillation profiles of the system such as period and number of cycles can be reliably regulated by the amount of cyclin B1 mRNAs.
source: The oscillation profiles of the system such as period and number of cycles can be reliably regulated by the amount of cyclin B1 mRNAs or sizes of droplets.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations showing regulation by cyclin B1 mRNA concentration.

claim: The oscillation profiles of the system such as period and number of cycles can be reliably regulated by sizes of droplets.
source: The oscillation profiles of the system such as period and number of cycles can be reliably regulated by the amount of cyclin B1 mRNAs or sizes of droplets.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations showing regulation by droplet size.

claim: Energy may be a critical factor for cell cycle behaviors.
source: Additionally, we found that energy may be a critical factor for cell cycle behaviors.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' findings from their experiments and modeling.

claim: The authors used a simple vortexing technique to compartmentalize reactions of cycling Xenopus egg extracts into microemulsion droplets.
source: To create a cell-like in vitro mitotic system, we used a simple vortexing technique (Ho et al., 2017) to compartmentalize reactions of cycling Xenopus egg extracts (Murray, 1991) into microemulsion droplets, with radii ranging from 10 µm to 300 µm (Figure 1B, Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used by the authors, with a citation to Ho et al., 2017 for the vortexing technique.

claim: The microemulsion droplets have radii ranging from 10 µm to 300 µm.
source: To create a cell-like in vitro mitotic system, we used a simple vortexing technique (Ho et al., 2017) to compartmentalize reactions of cycling Xenopus egg extracts (Murray, 1991) into microemulsion droplets, with radii ranging from 10 µm to 300 µm (Figure 1B, Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' measurements of droplet sizes.

claim: The droplet system is capable of reconstructing at least three mitotic processes in parallel that alternate between interphase and mitosis.
source: We demonstrated that the system is capable of reconstructing at least three mitotic processes in parallel that alternate between interphase and mitosis (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 1 and video 1.

claim: The autonomous alternation of distinct cell-cycle phases is driven by a self-sustained oscillator, the activity of which was indicated by the periodic degradation of an anaphase substrate of APC/C, securin-mCherry.
source: The autonomous alternation of distinct cell-cycle phases is driven by a self-sustained oscillator, the activity of which was indicated by the periodic degradation of an anaphase substrate of APC/C, securin-mCherry.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations of securin-mCherry degradation.

claim: In interphase, the presence of sperm chromosomal DNA initiated the self-assembly of a nucleus.
source: In interphase, the presence of sperm chromosomal DNA, labeled by Hoechst, initiated the self-assembly of a nucleus, upon which GFP-NLS protein was imported through the nuclear pores.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations of nucleus assembly in the presence of sperm DNA.

claim: GFP-NLS protein was imported through the nuclear pores in interphase.
source: In interphase, the presence of sperm chromosomal DNA, labeled by Hoechst, initiated the self-assembly of a nucleus, upon which GFP-NLS protein was imported through the nuclear pores.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations of GFP-NLS localization.

claim: The spatial distributions of Hoechst and GFP-NLS coincided in an interphase nucleus.
source: The spatial distributions of Hoechst and GFP-NLS thus coincided in an interphase nucleus (Figure 1C columns 1, 3, and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: As the artificial cell entered mitosis, the chromosome condensed resulting in a tighter distribution of Hoechst.
source: As the artificial cell entered mitosis, the chromosome condensed resulting in a tighter distribution of Hoechst, while the nuclear envelope broke down and GFP-NLS quickly dispersed into a uniform distribution in the whole droplet (Figure 1C columns 2 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: As the artificial cell entered mitosis, the nuclear envelope broke down and GFP-NLS quickly dispersed into a uniform distribution in the whole droplet.
source: As the artificial cell entered mitosis, the chromosome condensed resulting in a tighter distribution of Hoechst, while the nuclear envelope broke down and GFP-NLS quickly dispersed into a uniform distribution in the whole droplet (Figure 1C columns 2 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The chromosome condensation and nuclear envelope breakdown (NEB) happened almost at the same time.
source: The time courses for these processes were analyzed in Figure 1D, indicating that the chromosome condensation and nuclear envelop breakdown (NEB) happened almost at the same time, while securin degradation lagged behind these two processes at each cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of time courses shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Securin degradation lagged behind chromosome condensation and nuclear envelope breakdown at each cycle.
source: The time courses for these processes were analyzed in Figure 1D, indicating that the chromosome condensation and nuclear envelop breakdown (NEB) happened almost at the same time, while securin degradation lagged behind these two processes at each cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis of time courses shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The droplet system successfully reconstituted a cell-free mitotic oscillator centered on Cdk1 and APC/C that can reliably drive the periodic progression of downstream events including chromosome morphology change and nuclear envelope breakdown and re-assembly.
source: All together, these experiments showed that the droplet system successfully reconstituted a cell-free mitotic oscillator centered on Cdk1 and APC/C that can reliably drive the periodic progression of downstream events including chromosome morphology change and nuclear envelope breakdown and re-assembly, like what occurs in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations of multiple mitotic processes in droplets.

claim: The ability to adjust frequency is an important feature shared by many oscillators.
source: The ability to adjust frequency is an important feature shared by many oscillators (Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2008.

claim: The minimal mitotic oscillatory system (cytoplasmic-only, without sperm chromatin) produced highly robust, undamped, self-sustained oscillations up to 32 cycles over a lifetime of 4 days.
source: This simple, cytoplasmic-only oscillator produced highly robust, undamped, self-sustained oscillations up to 32 cycles over a lifetime of 4 days (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—video 1), significantly better than many existing synthetic oscillators.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The cytoplasmic-only oscillator is significantly better than many existing synthetic oscillators.
source: This simple, cytoplasmic-only oscillator produced highly robust, undamped, self-sustained oscillations up to 32 cycles over a lifetime of 4 days (Figure 2A,B, Figure 2—video 1), significantly better than many existing synthetic oscillators.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' comparison of their system to existing synthetic oscillators.

claim: Cyclin B1-YFP and securin-mCherry both are reliable reporters for the cell cycle oscillator.
source: A droplet supplied with both cyclin B1-YFP and securin-mCherry mRNAs exhibited oscillations with highly correlated signals (Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 2), suggesting that both are reliable reporters for the oscillator activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations of correlated signals shown in Figure 2C.

claim: With an increased concentration of cyclin B1-YFP mRNAs added to the system, the average period decreased.
source: With an increased concentration of cyclin B1-YFP mRNAs added to the system, we observed a decrease in the average period (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1), meaning that a higher cyclin B1 concentration tends to speed up the oscillations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A higher cyclin B1 concentration tends to speed up the oscillations.
source: With an increased concentration of cyclin B1-YFP mRNAs added to the system, we observed a decrease in the average period (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1), meaning that a higher cyclin B1 concentration tends to speed up the oscillations.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of their experimental observations.

claim: The average number of cycles was reduced with increased cyclin B1 concentrations.
source: However, the average number of cycles (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 1) was also reduced with increased cyclin B1 concentrations, resulting in a negative correlation between the lifetime of oscillations and the amount of cyclin B1 mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is a negative correlation between the lifetime of oscillations and the amount of cyclin B1 mRNAs.
source: However, the average number of cycles (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 1) was also reduced with increased cyclin B1 concentrations, resulting in a negative correlation between the lifetime of oscillations and the amount of cyclin B1 mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' analysis of their experimental data.

claim: The extracts will eventually arrest at a mitotic phase in the presence of high concentrations of cyclin B1.
source: The extracts will eventually arrest at a mitotic phase in the presence of high concentrations of cyclin B1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Smaller droplets led to slower oscillations with a larger variance of the periods.
source: Figure 2F (Figure 2—source data 2) showed that smaller droplets led to slower oscillations with a larger variance of the periods, consistent with the size effect reported on an in vitro transcriptional oscillator (Weitz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The size effect on oscillation period is consistent with the size effect reported on an in vitro transcriptional oscillator.
source: Figure 2F (Figure 2—source data 2) showed that smaller droplets led to slower oscillations with a larger variance of the periods, consistent with the size effect reported on an in vitro transcriptional oscillator (Weitz et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weitz et al., 2014.

claim: Smaller droplets exhibited a reduced number of oscillations and a smaller variance of the cycle number.
source: We also observed a reduced number of oscillations and a smaller variance of the cycle number in smaller droplets (Figure 2G, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The size effects become less dramatic for droplets with larger sizes or with higher concentrations of cyclin B1 mRNAs.
source: Interestingly, these size effects become less dramatic for droplets with larger sizes or with higher concentrations of cyclin B1 mRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: Securin-mCherry and cyclin B1-YFP both exhibited oscillations of increased amplitude, baseline, and period over time.
source: Moreover, we have observed that securin-mCherry and cyclin B1-YFP both exhibited oscillations of increased amplitude, baseline, and period over time (Figure 2C), of which the increasing period over time is evident by analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations shown in Figure 2C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The trends of increasing amplitude, baseline, and period over time cannot be explained by existing cell cycle models.
source: Moreover, we have observed that securin-mCherry and cyclin B1-YFP both exhibited oscillations of increased amplitude, baseline, and period over time (Figure 2C), of which the increasing period over time is evident by analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B. These trends cannot be explained by existing cell cycle models (Yang and Ferrell, 2013; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' comparison of their observations to existing models cited.

claim: Cell-free extracts lack yolk as an energy source.
source: Unlike intact embryos, cell-free extracts lack yolk as an energy source and lack sufficient mitochondria for energy regeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the composition of cell-free extracts compared to intact embryos.

claim: Cell-free extracts lack sufficient mitochondria for energy regeneration.
source: Unlike intact embryos, cell-free extracts lack yolk as an energy source and lack sufficient mitochondria for energy regeneration.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the composition of cell-free extracts.

claim: Energy is an important regulator for a droplet system with a limited amount of energy source consumed over time.
source: We postulated that energy is an important regulator for a droplet system with a limited amount of energy source consumed over time.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' hypothesis about the role of energy in their system.

claim: The energy depletion model is based on a well-established cell-cycle model modified by introducing ATP into all phosphorylation reactions.
source: The energy depletion model is based on a well-established cell-cycle model (Yang and Ferrell, 2013; Tsai et al., 2014) modified by introducing ATP into all phosphorylation reactions (Figure 3A, Materials and methods 8 and 9).
evidence: The claim describes the authors' modeling approach, which is based on prior models with modifications.

claim: Decreasing the ATP concentration leads to a higher R value (ratio of Wee1 to Cdc25 activity).
source: Relationship between ATP percentage and R value, showing that decreasing the ATP concentration leads to a higher R value.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At a low r (e.g. 0.5), the system stays at a stable steady-state with low cyclin B concentration.
source: In Figure 3C, the phase plot of the two-ODE model shows that at a low r (e.g. 0.5), the system stays at a stable steady-state with low cyclin B concentration and at a high r (e.g. 2.5), the oscillation is arrested at a stable steady-state with high cyclin B concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At a high r (e.g. 2.5), the oscillation is arrested at a stable steady-state with high cyclin B concentration.
source: In Figure 3C, the phase plot of the two-ODE model shows that at a low r (e.g. 0.5), the system stays at a stable steady-state with low cyclin B concentration and at a high r (e.g. 2.5), the oscillation is arrested at a stable steady-state with high cyclin B concentration.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At an intermediate value, increasing r can produce oscillations of increased amplitude, baseline and period.
source: At an intermediate value, increasing r can produce oscillations of increased amplitude, baseline and period (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: If the available ATP concentration decreases over time, the model can readily recapitulate the experimentally observed increment of amplitude, baseline, and period of the cyclin B time course.
source: If we assume that the available ATP concentration decreases over time, we can readily recapitulate the experimentally observed increment of amplitude, baseline, and period of the cyclin B time course (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The energy depletion model can predict the experimental observations that both period and number of cycles decrease with increasing cyclin B concentration.
source: The energy depletion model can also predict the experimental observations in Figure 2D and E by showing that both period and number of cycles decrease with increasing cyclin B concentration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The changes of synthesis and degradation rates yielded no obvious effects on the amplitude and baseline.
source: However, the changes of synthesis and degradation rates yielded no obvious effects on the amplitude and baseline (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The authors have developed a novel artificial cell system that enables highly robust and tunable mitotic oscillations.
source: We have developed here a novel artificial cell system that enables highly robust and tunable mitotic oscillations.
evidence: The claim summarizes the authors' main contribution based on their experimental results.

claim: The system is amenable to high throughput, quantitative manipulation and analysis of both cytoplasmic and nuclear processes.
source: The system is amenable to high throughput, quantitative manipulation and analysis of both cytoplasmic and nuclear processes.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' characterization of their system's capabilities.

claim: Cell cycles share common topologies with many biological oscillators.
source: Given cell cycles share common topologies with many biological oscillators, the system may be valuable to investigate fundamental principles of oscillator theory.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the similarity of cell cycle networks to other oscillators.

claim: The system may be valuable to investigate fundamental principles of oscillator theory.
source: Given cell cycles share common topologies with many biological oscillators, the system may be valuable to investigate fundamental principles of oscillator theory.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the potential applications of the system.

claim: The energy depletion model suggests an interesting mechanism to modulate oscillations with a single control parameter r that depends on the energy-tunable balance of two positive feedback loops.
source: Our energy depletion model suggested an interesting mechanism to modulate oscillations with a single control parameter r that depends on the energy-tunable balance of two positive feedback loops.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' modeling results and interpretation.

claim: The rapid, synchronous cleavages of an early embryo require a large amount of energy that remains unchanged for the first cleavage stages before rapidly dropping until the mid-blastula stage when cell cycles slow down.
source: Considering that the rapid, synchronous cleavages of an early embryo require a large amount of energy that remains unchanged for the first cleavage stages before rapidly dropping until the mid-blastula stage when cell cycles slow down (Zotin et al., 1967), this energy-dependent control may function as a 'checkpoint' to regulate cell cycles when r becomes large.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zotin et al., 1967.

claim: Energy-dependent control may function as a 'checkpoint' to regulate cell cycles when r becomes large.
source: Considering that the rapid, synchronous cleavages of an early embryo require a large amount of energy that remains unchanged for the first cleavage stages before rapidly dropping until the mid-blastula stage when cell cycles slow down (Zotin et al., 1967), this energy-dependent control may function as a 'checkpoint' to regulate cell cycles when r becomes large.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the authors' model and cited observations.

claim: The cyclin B-Cdk1 complex activates its own activator, phosphatase Cdc25, forming a positive feedback loop.
source: The central regulator, cyclin B-Cdk1 complex activates its own activator, phosphatase Cdc25, forming a positive feedback loop, and inhibits its own inhibitor, kinase Wee1, forming a double negative feedback loop.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of cell cycle regulation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The cyclin B-Cdk1 complex inhibits its own inhibitor, kinase Wee1, forming a double negative feedback loop.
source: The central regulator, cyclin B-Cdk1 complex activates its own activator, phosphatase Cdc25, forming a positive feedback loop, and inhibits its own inhibitor, kinase Wee1, forming a double negative feedback loop.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of cell cycle regulation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CyclinB-Cdk1 activates the E3 ubiquitin ligase APC/C, which targets cyclin B for degradation and completes a core negative feedback loop.
source: Additionally, cyclinB-Cdk1 activates the E3 ubiquitin ligase APC/C, which targets cyclin B for degradation and completes a core negative feedback loop.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of cell cycle regulation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Active APC/C promotes the degradation of another substrate securin.
source: Active APC/C also promotes the degradation of another substrate securin.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of APC/C substrates shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Once cyclinB1-Cdk1 complex is activated, the circuit drives a set of mitotic events including chromosome condensation and nuclear envelope breakdown (NEB).
source: Once cyclinB1-Cdk1 complex is activated, the circuit drives a set of mitotic events including chromosome condensation and nuclear envelope breakdown (NEB).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of mitotic events shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cycling Xenopus extracts are supplemented with various combinations of recombinant proteins, mRNAs, and de-membraned sperm DNAs, which are encapsulated in 2% Perfluoropolyether-poly (ethylene glycol) (PFPE-PEG) oil microemulsions.
source: Cycling Xenopus extracts are supplemented with various combinations of recombinant proteins, mRNAs, and de-membraned sperm DNAs, which are encapsulated in 2% Perfluoropolyether-poly (ethylene glycol) (PFPE-PEG) oil microemulsions.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The cyclic progression of the cell cycle clock and its downstream mitotic processes are simultaneously tracked by multiple fluorescence reporters.
source: The cyclic progression of the cell cycle clock and its downstream mitotic processes are simultaneously tracked by multiple fluorescence reporters.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental approach shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The clock regulator APC/C activity is reported by its substrate securin-mCherry.
source: The clock regulator APC/C activity is reported by its substrate securin-mCherry, chromosomal morphology changes by the Hoechst stains, and NEB by GFP-NLS.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental reporters used, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Chromosomal morphology changes are reported by the Hoechst stains.
source: The clock regulator APC/C activity is reported by its substrate securin-mCherry, chromosomal morphology changes by the Hoechst stains, and NEB by GFP-NLS.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental reporters used, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nuclear envelope breakdown is reported by GFP-NLS.
source: The clock regulator APC/C activity is reported by its substrate securin-mCherry, chromosomal morphology changes by the Hoechst stains, and NEB by GFP-NLS.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental reporters used, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nuclear envelopes are detectable on bright field images, matching the localization of GFP-NLS indicated nuclei.
source: Nuclear envelopes (red arrows) are also detectable on bright field images, matching the localization of GFP-NLS indicated nuclei.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Chromosome condensation happens almost at the same time as the nuclear envelope breaks down.
source: Chromosome condensation happens almost at the same time as the nuclear envelope breaks down (black dashed line).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Degradation of the APC/C substrate lags behind NEB consistently at each cycle.
source: The red dashed line represents the intensity of securin-mCherry over time, suggesting that degradation of the APC/C substrate lags behind NEB consistently at each cycle.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Extracts with cyclin B mRNA concentrations above 10 ng/µL did not exhibit sustained oscillations before arresting at a mitotic phase.
source: Extracts with cyclin B mRNA concentrations above 10 ng/µL did not exhibit sustained oscillations before arresting at a mitotic phase.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental observations.

claim: At the scale of a cell, the dynamics of biochemical reactions may become stochastic.
source: At the scale of a cell, the dynamics of biochemical reactions may become stochastic.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about stochastic effects at small scales.

claim: Studying a stochastic system that is out of steady-state can be challenging in living organism due to low throughput and complications from cell growth, divisions and other complex cellular environments.
source: Although stochastic phenomenon has been studied extensively in genetic expressions, studying a stochastic system that is out of steady-state can be challenging in living organism due to low throughput and complications from cell growth, divisions and other complex cellular environments.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reasoning about the challenges of studying stochastic out-of-steady-state systems in vivo.

claim: The limitations of studying stochastic out-of-steady-state systems can be overcome by reconstitution of in vitro oscillators inside cell-scale droplets, which are in absence of cell growth and divisions.
source: These limitations can be overcome by reconstitution of in vitro oscillators inside cell-scale droplets, which are in absence of cell growth and divisions.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reasoning about the advantages of their droplet system.

claim: Parallel tracking of droplets enables high-throughput data generation for statistical analysis.
source: Parallel tracking of droplets also enables high-throughput data generation for statistical analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' characterization of their experimental approach.

claim: In vitro compartmentalization of molecules, especially rate-limiting molecules such as cyclin B1 mRNAs, into cell-sized droplets may have a major effect on the reaction kinetics of cell cycles.
source: In vitro compartmentalization of molecules, especially rate-limiting molecules such as cyclin B1 mRNAs, into cell-sized droplets may have a major effect on the reaction kinetics of cell cycles.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reasoning about the effects of compartmentalization.

claim: The smaller the size of a droplet, the smaller the copy number of molecules encapsulated inside the droplet and the larger the inherent stochasticity of biochemical reactions.
source: The smaller the size of a droplet, the smaller the copy number of molecules encapsulated inside the droplet and the larger the inherent stochasticity of biochemical reactions.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about stochastic effects in small volumes.

claim: The partition errors of molecules resulted from compartmentalization may further contribute to the variations of droplet behaviors in a size-dependent manner.
source: Additionally, the partition errors of these molecule resulted from compartmentalization may further contribute to the variations of droplet behaviors in a size-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' reasoning about sources of variation in droplet behavior.

claim: The balance between Wee1 and Cdc25 activity was suggested to be crucial for the transition of cell cycle status during early embryo development.
source: In the cell cycle network, the activation of Cdk1 is co-regulated by a double positive feedback through a phosphatase Cdc25 and a double negative feedback through a kinase Wee1. The balance between Wee1 and Cdc25 activity was suggested to be crucial for the transition of cell cycle status during early embryo development (Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2014.

claim: ATP-dependent phosphorylation of Cdc25 and Wee1 can decrease R by activating Cdc25 and inhibiting Wee1 simultaneously.
source: We noted that ATP-dependent phosphorylation of Cdc25 and Wee1 can decrease R by activating Cdc25 and inhibiting Wee1 simultaneously, resulting in a high dependence of R on the ATP concentration (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: ATP-dependent phosphorylation of Cdc25 and Wee1 results in a high dependence of R on the ATP concentration.
source: We noted that ATP-dependent phosphorylation of Cdc25 and Wee1 can decrease R by activating Cdc25 and inhibiting Wee1 simultaneously, resulting in a high dependence of R on the ATP concentration (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' modeling results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cycling Xenopus extracts were prepared as described by Murray, 1991, except that eggs were activated with calcium ionophore A23187 (200 ng/µL) rather than electric shock.
source: Cycling Xenopus extracts were prepared as described (Murray, 1991), except that eggs were activated with calcium ionophore A23187 (200 ng/µL) rather than electric shock.
